Tutorials

  • A coding agent on a machine

#Config

serviceman reads one JSON file, data/serviceman.json: bin/configure writes a starting one when there is none, and bin/run hands it to the image. Every relative path inside the file is read against the folder the file lives in. Run on the machine itself, node src/main takes the path from the command line, from $SERVICEMAN_CONFIG, or it is ./serviceman.json.

node src/main                                # ./serviceman.json
node src/main /etc/serviceman.json
node src/main data/serviceman.json --check   # read the config, report what is wrong, exit

--check refuses a config that would only fail at the first request: an unknown type, a missing image, a hostname written twice, a duration nobody can read.

#Edit from the control page

Services are created and reshaped on the control page itself. + Add service asks what it is — a docker image, a program, or something already running — and opens the cards it cannot do without; the name comes from the image and the port defaults to the one the image names, or 80, when left empty, and an address with a path strips its prefix. A service's own page is the same cards, each with Edit — addresses, image, storage, environment, the whole policy. A card's Save writes the config file and applies it at once; only the fields you fill land in the file. Remove…, the last card, takes a service out of the config — anything running keeps running.

Everything in this file has a place on that page: Runs on is a list of machines and #tags in the order they are tried, Follow the load turns the autoscaler on under Copies, the checkbox beside the image fetches it before the first visit, a remote's Tags sit in its form, and Let machines join on the Remotes page holds the join token and the tags a machine may claim.

For the edge cases the pencil opens the config file in a code editor. Check reads the text and reports what is wrong without touching anything. Save writes the file and applies it the same way:

  • A service whose definition did not change keeps running untouched.
  • A new or changed service starts fresh; a changed one gets its container replaced at the next start.
  • A removed service is no longer served, but anything running keeps running.
  • listen and control are saved but wait for a serviceman restart.

A save is refused while the file on disk differs from what the editor loaded — someone edited it in parallel. Load it again and repeat the edit.

#The whole file

{
    "listen": {"host": "127.0.0.1", "port": 8080, "socket": null},
    "control": {"host": "serviceman.localhost", "port": 8081, "bind": "127.0.0.1", "socket": null},
    "defaults": {"start": "on_demand", "stop_after_idle": "10m", "start_timeout": "120s"},
    "remotes": [],
    "services": []
}
Field Default What it is
listen 127.0.0.1:8080 Where the services are served: a port, a socket file, or both.
control see below Where the control page is.
defaults see the table below The policy every service starts from.
remotes [] The machines that carry services. See below.
logline none Where the remotes send their logs. See Logline below.
load_tests [] What k6 is sent at. See Load tests at the end.
services required The list below.

#A socket file instead of a port

Either door can be a file on disk as well as a port:

"listen": {"host": "127.0.0.1", "port": 8080, "socket": "run/services.sock"},
"control": {"host": "serviceman.localhost", "port": null, "socket": "run/control.sock"}

The services are answered by hostname through the file exactly as through the port:

curl --unix-socket run/services.sock http://grafana.example.com/

A socket file needs no port and no address of its own, and ssh -L /here.sock:/there.sock moves it between machines — so the control page, or a whole set of services, can be reached from your laptop with nothing open on the box, and an agent can dial in the same way (--url unix:///run/control.sock). It is also the answer to fronting something with socat: serviceman speaks the socket itself.

Who may open the file is who may knock, so socket_mode is the whole of its security — 0600 by default, the owner and nobody else. A stale file from a serviceman that died is taken over; a file something still answers on is left alone and serviceman refuses to start.

Both doors are on the loopback until you say otherwise. listen.host is the address the services are served on; nothing outside the machine reaches them until it is widened, usually to 0.0.0.0 behind a TLS terminator.

control.host is a hostname on the service port; control.port is a second port that serves the control page and nothing else. Set either to null to close that door.

Field Default What it is
host see above The hostname that reaches the control page over the service port.
port 8081 A port of its own for the control page. null closes it.
bind 127.0.0.1 The address that port is bound to.
socket none A socket file the control page also answers on. See below.
socket_mode "0600" Who may open that file, and so who may reach the page through it.
exposed false Answer callers other than this machine. See below.
names [] Other hostnames the control page may be asked by, when something renames it.
shell true false keeps the page and takes the Shell button away.

The control page reads and writes the config, opens shells inside containers and holds the remote tokens, and it asks for no password. So it answers the machine serviceman runs on and nobody else: asked from anywhere else, over either port, it is a 404 like any unknown address. Reach it through an ssh tunnel, or set "exposed": true and put your own wall in front — serviceman says that out loud at startup when you do.

control.names only widens which hostnames it answers by, never which callers. A caller that is not this machine is still refused.

The Shell of a container asks the docker socket on the machine that runs it, through the agent's link; the agent says where that socket is.

#Remotes

A remote is a machine that carries services — a VPS, or the very machine serviceman runs on. It runs the agent, which dials this host and waits for orders; serviceman itself starts nothing and runs no docker. + Add remote on the control page writes this block for you. serviceman never dials out, so the machine needs no open port, no public address and no key of yours. Remotes has the whole story — installing the agent, a systemd unit, and what the token buys.

"remotes": [
    {"name": "vps1", "title": "Example VPS", "token": "0c0f…a91b", "tags": ["gpu", "eu"]}
]
Field What it is
name Lowercase letters, digits, - and _. The agent dials in under this name.
title The name on the control page. Optional.
token The secret the agent proves itself with. At least 16 characters.
tags What this machine is, for a service that asks for a kind of machine.
machine Written by serviceman when a machine adds itself; see A machine that adds itself.
logs "all" sends every container's output to Logline; "off", the default, sends none. See Logline.
log_dirs Folders whose files go to Logline as well, while logs is "all": [{"path": "/var/log/nginx/*.log", "service": "nginx"}].

The token lets another machine run programs for you, so make it a real one:

openssl rand -hex 32

On the other machine, with node installed:

serviceman-agent --url https://serviceman.example.com --token 0c0f…a91b

The agent says what the machine has — cpu, memory, free disk, docker version — and repeats the numbers that move every 30 seconds. This host pings it every 30 seconds for the delay, and sends a megabyte there and back every ten minutes for the speed. A link that stops answering is dropped; the agent dials in again, waiting 1s, then 2s, up to 30s.

A remote that keeps its name and its token keeps its link when the config is applied again. Changing either drops the link, and the agent comes back with the new one.

#Logline

Logline is where the remotes' logs go: one endpoint, and ClickHouse behind it. serviceman says where it is, and asks it for the token each machine sends its lines with.

It is typed in on any machine's Logs tab, under Where Logline is — the endpoint, the admin token and the viewer — and written here; the admin token goes to the Secrets library.

"logline": {"endpoint": "http://logline:3000/lines", "admin": "logline"}
Field What it is
endpoint Where the machines POST their lines.
admin The name of a secret in the Secrets library holding Logline's ADMIN_TOKEN. The value is never in the config.
ui Where Logline's viewer is, such as http://logline:8081/. Optional: the Logline button on a machine's Logs tab opens it.

A remote with "logs": "all" is told the endpoint and a token of its own. Logline binds that token to the machine's addresses, which the agent says when it dials in; the token works from those addresses and nowhere else. serviceman keeps the tokens it was given in data/logline_tokens.json, mode 600, and takes a token back when its remote leaves the config.

The moment a machine is switched on is its floor: every line from then on is kept, and none from before. The agent writes the floor down before anything else, in <agent folder>/logline/settings.json, so a restart does not move it. Switching logs on or off is told over the link the machine is on; it does not dial in again. The machine's Logs tab switches it, and says where its lines go, from when, how many went and how many wait, and why the last telling failed if it did.

A machine switched on follows every container it has — the ones there, the ones stopped, and every one started later — from its floor, into a spool on its own disk, and sends the spool to Logline in batches. A batch leaves the spool only when Logline has it; while Logline cannot be reached the spool grows, up to a gigabyte or a tenth of the disk, and then the machine stops reading and docker keeps the lines until there is room. A container labelled logline=off is left alone. The agent's own lines go too — what it connected to, what it was asked, what went wrong — labelled service=serviceman-agent, from the moment collection starts, the lines it wrote just before that included. How it is kept from losing or repeating a line is in notes/logline.md.

Folders go besides the containers, set on the same tab: a folder — every file in it — or a folder and a pattern, /var/log/nginx/*.log, from / or ~/. Files already there when a folder is added are read from where they end then; files that appear later are read from their start, a line at a time as they are written. A file is known by its inode, so logrotate's rename keeps it, and one truncated in place is read again from its start. Compressed and hidden files are left alone. Each line is labelled host, service — the name given, or the folder's own — and file. serviceman's own log is one such folder: its data/logs, read by the agent on the machine serviceman runs on.

#A service on a remote

{
    "name": "grafana",
    "type": "docker",
    "remotes": ["vps1", "vps2"],
    "publish": {"host": "grafana.example.com", "port": 3000},
    "image": "grafana/grafana:latest"
}

Every docker and shell service belongs to a remote: remotes lists the machines it may run on, best first, and one of them is required — a container and a program run where an agent is, and nowhere else. "remote": "vps1" is shorthand for a list of one. An external service names none: it already runs somewhere, on no machine of ours.

When an instance starts, serviceman reserves a machine: the first one on the list that is online, written down before anything is started, and kept for the life of that copy. A machine that fails to start it is crossed off and the next one is tried. Nothing moves by itself afterwards — a running instance stays where it is until it stops.

The address stays here; the container runs there. serviceman drives docker over the link — run, start, stop, inspect, logs — and every request rides back through the same link, so the remote needs no open port. The visitor sees no difference.

While the agent is away the service is out of reach: what already runs over there keeps running, and a request gets remote vps1 is offline — no machine to start it on. When the agent dials in again, a container still running is adopted, not started twice, and a service with "start": "always" is started then.

A folder in volumes is a folder on the remote's machine, and the agent makes it if it is missing. Write it as an absolute path — a relative one is read against the config folder on this host, which means nothing over there.

#A kind of machine instead of one machine

A service names the machines it may run on, best first — and a #tag stands for every machine carrying it:

{"name": "grafana", "type": "docker", "remotes": ["#gpu"], "image": "grafana/grafana:latest"}
{"name": "api", "type": "docker", "remotes": ["vps1", "#eu"], "image": "demo/api"}

The second one prefers vps1 and falls back to anything tagged eu.

Tags come from two places: this file, and the machine itself — serviceman-agent --tag gpu, which holds while its link does. So a tag nothing carries yet is not an error at load; the boot writes serviceman_tag_nowhere for it, and the service waits for a machine that answers.

#A machine that adds itself

One secret lets a machine nobody has written down join the fleet:

"join": {"token": "0c0f…a91b", "tags_allowed": ["gpu", "eu"], "name_prefix": "auto-"}

serviceman-agent --url https://serviceman.example.com --token <the join token> --tag gpu

serviceman writes the new machine into this file — with a secret of its own, the tags it was allowed to claim, and the machine it says it is — and it appears on the control page like any other. The same machine coming back takes its own entry again instead of leaving a dead one.

A tag in the config is a fact; a tag from a machine is a claim. A machine may only claim what tags_allowed lists; anything else is dropped and written to the log. The join token is the trust boundary of the fleet — whoever holds it gets a machine in and the work that goes with it — so it is a password, not a setting. Leave join out and no machine can add itself, which is the default.

#A service

{
    "name": "grafana",
    "title": "Grafana",
    "type": "docker",
    "publish": {"host": "grafana.example.com", "port": 3000},
    "policy": {"start": "on_demand", "stop_after_idle": "30m", "start_timeout": "90s"}
}
Field What it is
name Lowercase letters, digits, - and _. It names the container and the API path.
title The name on the control page and on the waiting page. Optional.
type docker, shell or external.
publish Everything outside: the address it answers on, and the port behind it.
remotes The machines it may run on, best first. Required for docker and shell; none for the rest.
redirect Wake it, then send the visitor to this address instead of proxying. Optional.
policy The fields below.

Everything else in a service says how it is run: the image, the command, the address it already answers on.

#publish

Field What it is
host One address. Use hosts for a list. *.example.com matches every name under it.
port The port the service listens on inside the container, the stack or the program.
strip_prefix The service behind a path prefix sees paths without it.

Exact hostnames win over wildcards. An address belongs to one service only. A program that answers nowhere has no publish at all.

#Addresses with a path

An address is a hostname with an optional path prefix:

{"name": "pdf", "type": "docker", "publish": {"host": "tools.example.com/pdf", "port": 3000}, ...}
{"name": "img", "type": "docker", "publish": {"host": "tools.example.com/img", "port": 3000}, ...}
{"name": "www", "type": "external", "publish": {"host": "tools.example.com"}, "upstream": "127.0.0.1:7000"}

One hostname is shared by many services this way. The longest matching prefix wins: /pdf/report goes to the pdf service, /img/logo.png to the img service, everything else to the www service. /pdf claims /pdf and everything under /pdf/ — never /pdfx. Without a root service on the hostname, an unclaimed path answers 404.

The service sees the path as the browser sent it: the pdf service above receives /pdf/report. Set "strip_prefix": true inside publish when the app expects to live at the root — the same request then reaches it as /report.

#An address serviceman keeps for a service

Every service with an address also has one of serviceman's own:

http://localhost:3000/redir/07c20748/auth/callback
  →  http://google-docs-writer.localhost:3000/auth/callback

Anything asked there is sent on to the service's own address, with the rest of the path and the whole query untouched, and nothing is started to answer it. The control page shows it on the service, ready to copy.

It exists for the rules other people have about addresses. Google will not take http://google-docs-writer.localhost:3000/auth/callback as an OAuth redirect — over plain http it accepts localhost and 127.0.0.1 and nothing else, and a name under localhost is not localhost. It will take http://localhost:3000/redir/<uid>/auth/callback, which lands here and finishes at the service's own name — where the browser has the app's session, which a proxy would have lost.

The uid follows the service's name and does not change.

#Wake it, then hand the visitor over

{
    "name": "google-docs-writer",
    "type": "shell",
    "publish": {"host": "google-docs-writer.localhost", "port": 8090},
    "cwd": "/home/user/google-docs-writer",
    "argv": ["node", "src/http.js"],
    "redirect": "http://localhost:8090"
}

http://google-docs-writer.localhost:3000/ is then a door, not a proxy: serviceman starts the program, waits until it answers, and sends the browser to http://localhost:8090/ with a 302. The path and the query come along, and the answer is never cached — the door has to be knocked on every time, or a browser would go straight to a service nobody woke.

This is for an app whose session belongs to an address of its own: a cookie, or an OAuth callback registered with somebody else, that only works on localhost:8090. The door gives it a name; the app keeps its own origin.

serviceman sees nothing after the handover. The visitor talks to the service directly, so there is no honest idle clock: stop_after_idle is off for a handover service unless it asks for one itself, and then it counts from the last visitor through the door, not from the last thing the app did.

Whoever sees the traffic can stop the service — and that is the app now. An app that exits by itself after a quiet spell is marked stopped by serviceman (a clean exit is not restarted), and the next visitor through the door starts it again.

Only a service that is started for a visitor can carry a redirect: docker, shell.

#type: shell

The agent runs the command on its machine and keeps it alive:

{
    "name": "clickhouse-socket",
    "type": "shell",
    "command": "socat UNIX-LISTEN:/srv/clickhouse.sock,fork,unlink-early,mode=666 TCP:127.0.0.1:8081",
    "policy": {"start": "always", "restart": "always"}
}
Field What it is
command The line, run through /bin/sh -c. Pipes and redirections work.
argv The program and its arguments, when no shell is wanted. Wins over command.
image The environment its lines run in. Without one they run on the machine itself.
volumes The paths it keeps across starts. A service with any runs on one named machine.
user Who it is inside that image: node:node, 1000:1000. Default: whoever runs the agent, by number.
lifecycle A line for each moment of its life. See below.
cwd Where it runs. The config's folder — or one of serviceman's own when it installs itself.
env Added to the environment serviceman itself has.

#The lifecycle of a program

{
    "name": "google-docs-writer",
    "type": "shell",
    "remote": "laptop",
    "publish": {"host": "google-docs-writer.example.com", "port": 8090},
    "command": "bin/run",
    "lifecycle": {
        "install": "git clone https://github.com/vbarbarosh/google-docs-writer . && npm install && bin/configure",
        "update": "git pull && npm install",
        "stop": "bin/flush",
        "uninstall": "dropdb google_docs_writer"
    }
}

command is what the service is — the line that runs and keeps running. The lines in lifecycle are the moments around it, each run in cwd through /bin/sh -c, on the machine that carries the program:

Line When it runs
install The folder is not there yet. Once — the folder is marked with the line that made it. It always runs in an empty folder.
update The folder is there and the install line has changed. Without it, install runs again.
stop Before the program is stopped, for any reason. SERVICEMAN_REASON says which.
uninstall The service is gone from the config. It is stopped first, then this runs. For what the program made elsewhere — a database, a registration. Not for its folder.

#Fetching a program again

The program moved on — a commit was pushed — and the config did not change, so serviceman has no reason to notice. Fetch again on its page (POST /api/v1/services/<name>/update) is how you say so: it stops the service if it runs, runs the update line, or the install line in an empty folder when there is no update line, and starts it again if it was running.

Nothing else about the service moves. It keeps its name, its address, its folder — the name of that folder is made from the service's name, not from a moment in time — and its storage, which is a folder of its own beside it, never inside what an install empties. Which is to say: after a git clone install line runs again, the working copy is new and data/<service>/… is exactly what it was.

Whatever serviceman gave up on before is forgiven at that moment: a service that had used up its start attempts gets them back, because this is a different program now.

#Storage

A program that keeps something names the paths it keeps:

"volumes": [":/app/data"]

That is the whole of it — a path, and nothing to name. serviceman keeps it as a folder in the agent's own directory on the machine that runs the service:

~/serviceman-agent/data/<service>/app-data   →   /app/data

So everything the agent made is in one place and goes when the agent does, and bin/uninstall plus one rm -rf still leaves the machine as it was found. Everything else the program writes goes when it stops — including its own folder, which an install line empties.

A source before the path is still read, for the cases that need one: a name is a docker volume that other services may share ("shared:/mnt/things"), and something with a / is a path on that machine ("/srv/x:/data:ro").

A service that keeps something names one machine, and only one. What it keeps is on the machine that holds it and goes nowhere: a list of machines to fall back on would mean the same service coming up with somebody else's data, or with none, and a #tag would mean any machine at all. serviceman refuses both at config time rather than finding out later.

The Storage row on the control page lists everything kept, the machine each thing is on, and which services keep what in it.

#Secrets

A program that needs a key, a token or a client secret asks for it by name:

secrets credentials

serviceman keeps those values in data/secrets.json — mode 600, beside what it writes about itself, never in the config — and they are made on the control page, not in a file.

A secret made on a service's page is that service's own. Nothing else can read it, and it cannot be reused elsewhere: two services may both hold a token, and they are not the same token. The Secrets row in the rail holds a library beside them — values written down once, to be copied into as many services as need them. Copying happens on the host: a value that is kept here never goes out to a page and back.

At start, the secrets of a service are put on the machine that runs it — 600, in the agent's folder — with a secrets command beside them: on the program's PATH when it runs on the machine, mounted at /usr/local/bin/secrets when it runs in a container. A service with no secrets gets no file and no command at all.

#An image as the environment

{
    "name": "google-docs-writer",
    "type": "shell",
    "remote": "laptop",
    "image": "node:24-alpine",
    "publish": {"host": "google-docs-writer.example.com", "port": 8090},
    "command": "bin/run",
    "lifecycle": {"install": "npm install"}
}

With an image, every line runs inside a container of that image, with the program's folder mounted at /app and /app as the working folder. The install line becomes

docker run --rm --volume <folder>:/app --workdir /app node:24-alpine /bin/sh -c "npm install"

and the program itself becomes a container of serviceman's own, published like any other:

docker run -d --name serviceman-google-docs-writer --label serviceman.service=… \
    --volume <folder>:/app --workdir /app --publish 127.0.0.1::8090 \
    node:24-alpine /bin/sh -c "bin/run"

Nothing of ours runs in a container as root. The default is the user running serviceman or the agent, by number — --user 1000:1000 — because a container that writes into a mounted folder as root leaves a folder its owner cannot empty, cannot reinstall into and cannot take away. "user": "node:node" names one the image has instead, which is the tidier answer when the image was built with a user for the job. HOME is /app either way, so npm and its like have somewhere of their own to cache.

So the machine needs docker and nothing else — no node, no npm, no version of anything on it. From there it is an ordinary container of ours: the same stopping, the same finding it again after a restart. The folder stays on the machine, so what the install line writes into it outlives the container.

A program that installs itself gets a folder of serviceman's own. With no cwd in the config it is <name>.<suffix> — google-docs-writer.07c20748 — under data/services on this host, and under services in the agent's folder on a remote. The suffix follows the name and never changes, so update and every restart find the same folder, and nothing made there by hand can ever be mistaken for it.

An install always starts from nothing. A folder serviceman made is emptied before the install line runs, so git clone . means what it says, and it is taken away again if the line fails — half an install is worse than none, because the next try would meet its own leftovers and fail on those instead. A folder you named in cwd is never emptied and never removed; what an install line does in there is between you and it.

Uninstall means gone. A program that leaves the config is stopped — it is serviceman's own child, and leaving it would leave an orphan nobody adopts — and the folder serviceman made for it is removed with it. A folder you named in cwd is yours and is never touched: serviceman takes away only what it put there. On a remote the agent does the removing, and refuses any path that is not inside its own home.

What is left behind on a machine that was offline at that moment, or by a container of a service that was removed, is written down in orphans — a case that is not resolved yet.

A step that fails stops what it was part of: a failed install fails the start and the reason is on the waiting page. A failed stop line does not keep the program alive — it is signalled all the same, and the log carries what the line said.

There is no start line, because that is command, and no sleep or wake: a program that sleeps is a program that was stopped, and waking it is starting it again. Its stop line runs with SERVICEMAN_REASON=idle when the idle clock is what stopped it.

A program may name a remote or a #tag, the same as a container. The agent over there runs the install line, keeps the child, and serviceman reaches it down the same tunnel. What that machine needs is whatever the two lines need — for the one above, git and node.

With a publish.port the program is a service like any other: an address wakes it, the idle policy stops it. Without one it answers nowhere — a socket, a tunnel, a job — so it carries no publish at all and it starts with serviceman ("start": "always").

A program runs as one copy. The agent keeps the last of what it prints, and the waiting page reads it while the program comes up. The agent stops the whole process group, so a shell line takes its children with it.

serviceman stops the programs it started when it stops itself, through the agent. The agent holds the child, so a program outlives neither: an agent that is restarted answers that nothing of its runs, and the program is started again at the next request.

#Policy

Field Default What it does
start on_demand on_demand starts at the first request. always starts with serviceman.
stop_after_idle 10m Stops the service after this much quiet. false keeps it up.
start_timeout 120s How long a start may take to answer before it counts as failed.
start_tries 2 Starts that may fail in a row before serviceman stops trying.
request_timeout 60s A request with no answer for this long gets 504. false waits forever.
instances {min: 0, max: 1} How many copies of the service may run. See below.
concurrency unlimited Requests one instance takes at once. The rest wait in line.
warmup {queue: 1, wait: "2s"} When the line is long enough to start another instance.
scale_down_after 2m An extra instance with no work for this long is stopped.
restart on_failure What follows a program that stops by itself. See below.

Durations are 500ms, 30s, 10m, 2h, 1d. A plain number is seconds.

A service that cannot start is not asked forever. A broken command, a missing setting, an image that is not there — none of those get better by being tried again on every request, and each try repeats the whole cost: the clone, the install, the pull. After start_tries starts that failed in a row serviceman gives up (service_gave_up), and every request after that is answered from what is already known — no work, the same reason, at once.

Three things are a change, and each one lets it try again: you asking (the Start button, or POST /api/v1/services/<name>/start), its machine coming back, and its definition being edited. The log says so with service_try_again.

restart is on_failure (a bad exit code brings it back), always (any exit brings it back) or never. serviceman waits a second before the first restart and doubles the wait up to thirty seconds; a program that ran half a minute starts that count again. It applies to programs — a container is restarted by docker, through run_args.

An always service is never stopped by the idle policy. A service with requests in flight is never stopped either — the clock starts when the last one finishes.

#When a service counts as ready

serviceman asks the service for / and waits for an answer. Any answer counts — a 404 and a 500 are still something inside speaking HTTP — and the request goes through the same pool the visitors will use, so a service on a remote is asked down its own tunnel with the header user-agent: serviceman-probe.

An open port is not enough on purpose: docker publishes the port before the app inside binds it, so a socket that connects only proves docker is there, and the first visitor would meet a reset. A port that answers nothing for start_timeout fails the start, and the reason names the likely cause — is publish.port (5000) the port it listens on inside? A start that is merely slow says so in the log after ten seconds and carries on waiting.

#Stopping a service

policy.stop_timeout is how long a service is given to stop by itself before it is made to. Unset, each kind keeps its own: ten seconds for a container, which is what docker gives, and five for a program.

What is stopped is never one process. A shell line is a chain — bash → npm → sh → the server — and neither bash nor npm passes a signal on, so the process serviceman started is not the one holding the port. serviceman signals the whole process group and waits for the whole group: the stop is over when nothing of it is left, not when its first process went.

A service that takes the whole timeout every time it stops never received the signal at all. The log says so — program_killed for a program, container_killed for a container — and the cure is in the program, not in the timeout: a command that ends in exec is one process, and one process stops in milliseconds.

bin/run:  #!/bin/sh
          exec node src/http.js

exec npm start is not enough: npm makes its own child and drops the signal on the floor. notes/signals-through-a-process-chain.md has the measurements.

Every container serviceman makes is run with --init, because the trap has a second half: a program that is pid 1 of its container never receives a signal it has no handler for — the kernel throws it away, pid_namespaces(7) — so even a perfect exec chain would sit out the whole timeout. With --init docker's own init is pid 1 and the program is its child, with ordinary signal rules. The spec hash carries a version of the run line itself, so containers created before the flag are replaced on their next start — storage survives the replacement, anything written inside the container goes, as always.

#More than one instance

"policy": {
    "instances": {"min": 1, "max": 4},
    "concurrency": 10,
    "warmup": {"queue": 3, "wait": "1s"},
    "scale_down_after": "2m",
    "request_timeout": "30s"
}

With concurrency set, an instance takes that many requests at once and the rest wait in line. The line is what drives the pool:

  • A new instance starts when warmup.queue requests wait, or when one request has waited warmup.wait — whichever comes first, and only while fewer than instances.max are up.
  • A request that reaches request_timeout — waiting in line or waiting for the answer of the service — is answered with 504. The clock starts on an awake service; a cold start is start_timeout's business.
  • An extra instance with no work for scale_down_after is stopped. The pool never shrinks below instances.min (or below one, while the service is awake).
  • stop_after_idle still stops the whole service, instances.min included; the next request starts the first instance, and the rest of min warm up behind it.

Without concurrency there is no line, so the pool never grows by itself — warmup needs concurrency to mean anything.

#The pool follows the work

warmup grows the pool once visitors are already waiting. autoscale grows it before that, from how full the pool is:

"policy": {
    "instances": {"min": 1, "max": 6},
    "concurrency": 4,
    "autoscale": {"busy_up": 0.7, "up_for": "10s", "busy_down": 0.2, "down_for": "2m", "cool_down": "1m"}
}

busy is the share of the pool that is working — requests in flight and in line, over what the running copies can take at once. Every five seconds serviceman looks:

  • busy at or over busy_up for up_for — start as many copies as the load asks for, up to instances.max.
  • busy at or under busy_down for down_for — stop one copy, never below instances.min (or below one). The emptiest copy goes; one with a request in flight is left alone.
  • nothing at all for cool_down after a change — the pool cannot flap on one number.

The two thresholds must differ, and busy_down under busy_up is checked at load.

A slow start moves the line. A copy that took ten seconds to answer must be started before the pool is full, or every visitor after it waits through another ten. serviceman remembers how long the last copy took and lowers busy_up by 0.02 for every second of it, never below halfway to busy_down. The log says where the line stood: busy 0.82 of 0.50 for 12.000s.

Leave autoscale out and nothing scales by itself — warmup and scale_down_after behave exactly as before.

Extra containers are named serviceman-<name>-2, serviceman-<name>-3, and so on. Every instance of a docker service shares the same volumes — the service must be ready for that.

#type: docker

{
    "name": "grafana",
    "type": "docker",
    "publish": {"host": "grafana.example.com", "port": 3000},
    "image": "grafana/grafana:latest",
    "env": {"GF_SERVER_ROOT_URL": "https://grafana.example.com"},
    "volumes": ["/srv/grafana:/var/lib/grafana"],
    "network": "backend",
    "run_args": ["--memory", "512m"],
    "args": []
}
Field What it is
image Required. The image to run.
env Names and values for --env.
volumes Storage. See below.
network The docker network to join.
init false leaves docker's --init out, for an image that has to be pid 1 itself — one built on s6-overlay quits otherwise. Default true.
run_args Anything else for docker run, written as a list.
args The command line for the image itself.

serviceman runs docker run -d --name serviceman-<name> --label serviceman.service=<name> --publish 127.0.0.1::<port> .... Docker picks the host port, serviceman reads it back with docker port, so two services never fight over a number.

Pull on the service's page fetches the image again. A tag is not a version — :latest, or :24, or anything else somebody pushes over, is a name for whatever was published under it last — and a machine that already has an image by that name never asks again. This is the ask. Then it asks the container which image it was made from: where that is not the image the name stands for now — a different one came down, now or before, by this pull or by a docker pull on that machine — the container is taken away and made from the image the name stands for, and a service that was running is running again at the end. Where the container is already of that image, nothing is touched. POST /api/v1/services/<name>/pull is the same thing without the page.

The container is kept when the service stops, so the next start is a docker start and the logs stay. serviceman recreates the container when the definition changes — image, port, env, volumes, network, run_args or args. It carries the fingerprint of the definition as the serviceman.spec label and compares it at every start.

#What a start shows

A first start of a docker service is mostly a download, and a fat image is minutes of it. That is a step with a name of its own: the waiting page and the service page say

Downloading vbarbarosh/notes — 56% · 256.35MB of 458.43MB · 54.50MB/s · 4s left

with a bar that follows it, and the log keeps every line docker printed as docker_stdout.

The numbers come from docker itself, one layer at a time. Two things are worth knowing:

  • docker only draws progress for a terminal. Through a pipe it drops every message that carries a progress bar — see Display in moby's pkg/jsonmessage — so the pull is run through script -qefc '<docker> pull <image>' /dev/null, which gives it the terminal it is looking for. A machine without script (util-linux) still pulls; it just cannot say how far it is, and says so once as docker_pull_no_pty.
  • docker has no overall percentage, only per-layer bytes, and it names a layer's size only when that layer starts downloading. The percentage here counts the layers it has named and treats the ones it has not as an average of them — an estimate while it lasts, exact by the end. Without it the bar would walk backwards every time a new layer arrived.

Everything else a start does says so too: making the container from <image>, starting the container that is already here, and, past three seconds of silence, what is being waited for and whatever the service itself is writing.

#Storage

A service that keeps data gets a volumes list. The short form is a path and nothing else — the same line a program of the shell kind writes:

"volumes": [":/app/data"]

That says: this path survives the container being made again, and everything else the container writes goes with it. There is nothing to name — the agent keeps the folder itself, under its own directory on the machine that runs the container:

~/serviceman-agent/data/<service>/app-data   →   /app/data

A machine that runs a container with such a path needs an agent new enough to say where it lives; an older one is told to run bin/update and nothing is started with a path that cannot be resolved. A service that keeps anything runs on one named machine — the folder is there and goes nowhere, so remotes may not be a list or a #tag.

Write a source before the path for the cases that need one — a named volume other services share, a folder that already exists — as a string the way docker takes it, or as an object:

"volumes": [
    "grafana-data:/var/lib/grafana",
    "/srv/grafana/conf:/etc/grafana:ro",
    "data/uploads:/uploads",
    {"source": "/mnt/big/photos", "target": "/photos", "readonly": true, "create": false}
]
Field What it is
source A named docker volume, or a folder on that machine. Empty: a folder the agent keeps for this service.
target Where it appears inside the container. It starts with /.
readonly true adds :ro.
create Make the host folder if it is missing. true by default, ignored by named volumes.

A source with a / in it is a folder on the machine; a source without one is a named docker volume — the same rule docker uses. Write a folder as an absolute path: a relative one is read against the config folder on this host, which means nothing on the machine that runs the container. ~ is the agent's home.

The agent makes a missing folder before it starts the container. Without that, docker makes it as root and the service cannot write in it.

#type: external

{
    "name": "rockpool",
    "title": "Terminals",
    "type": "external",
    "publish": {"host": "terminals.example.com"},
    "upstream": "127.0.0.1:7000"
}

Something that already runs, and keeps running whatever serviceman does: another program with its own supervisor, a box on the network, a tool you start by hand. serviceman gives it an address and passes requests on.

Field What it is
upstream Required. Where it already answers, as host:port. Plain HTTP.
remote The machine it runs on, when that is one of the remotes. Optional.

#Something already running on a remote

With remote, upstream is an address on that machine, and serviceman reaches it through that machine's link, the way it reaches a service it started there. Nothing is opened on the machine and nothing else needs a route to it — a port bound to its loopback is enough.

{
    "name": "logline-ui",
    "title": "Logline",
    "type": "external",
    "remote": "server",
    "publish": {"host": "logline.localhost"},
    "upstream": "127.0.0.1:8081"
}

It is still never started or stopped. When the machine's link is down a visitor gets 502, the same as for a service that does not answer, and it answers again the moment the link is back.

It is never started, never stopped, never reaped — Start and Stop are refused, and only its cards are left on the control page. publish is the address it answers on here; there is no publish.port, because nothing has a port inside. When it stops answering a visitor gets 502 and the address stays as written, since there is nothing serviceman could restart.

#Load tests

A load test sends k6 at a service: a number of users asking for one address for a while. The Load tests page makes them, runs them and keeps what each run measured; this is the list it writes.

"load_tests": [
    {"name": "whoami", "service": "whoami", "remote": "laptop", "vus": 20, "duration": "30s", "p95_ms": 500, "errors_pct": 1}
]
Field What it is
name Required. Lowercase letters, digits, - and _.
service Required. The service it measures; it is woken before the clock starts.
remote Required. The remote k6 runs on, as the grafana/k6 container, removed when it is done.
url The address asked. Optional: without it, the service's first address on listen.
vus Required. Users asking at once, 1 to 1000; each asks again as soon as it is answered.
duration Required. How long it runs, 1s to 1h.
p95_ms It passes when 95% of the answers came faster than this. Optional.
errors_pct It passes when no more than this share of the answers failed. Optional.

k6 runs with the remote's own network, so a name under .localhost is that remote's loopback: to reach serviceman's listen there, run it from the remote on the machine serviceman runs on. A public name works from any of them. The last 20 runs of each test are kept in data/load_test_runs.json.
